newsitem.title: USA: New ways needed to control port pollution - report.
newsitem.headline: New ways needed to control port pollution - report.

text.p: Ports, regulators and communities need to revise the way they manage contaminated marine sediment and put more effort into controlling pollution sources, the National Research Council said Wednesday.

A report by the research body chartered by Congress said ports have been forced to bear too much of the responsibility and costs for managing tainted sediment, and more effort should be made to stop the contamination by dioxin, trace metals and other toxic substances.
The Environmental Protection Agency and state authorities should have a bigger role in identifying industries and other sources of the polluted sediment, the report said.

It also said regulators and ports should make more use of legal and enforcement tools to help control sources of the pollution that has stalled essential waterway maintenance and construction at many ports.

An estimated 5 to 10 percent of dredged sediments are contaminated, and there are no new technologies on the horizon to treat large volumes of contaminated sediment safely and economically, the report said.

The report said regulations on managing contaminated sediment tend to emphasize the mechanics of the task, such as how to excavate or remove them. Because of this, it said the importance of balancing risks and costs of different options often are overlooked.

The EPA and the U.S. Army Corp of Engineers, the two main federal agencies in this issue, should develop consistent procedures dealing with environmental and human health risks that stem from various management options, the report said.

While most aspects of handling tainted sediment are regulated at the local, state or federal level, the report said the rules may be conflicting and can block efforts to use the best management practices.
Managing contaminated sediment does not necessarily involve removing it, the report said.
At some sites, allowing sediment to be gradually buried or decomposed, or capping it with a layer of clean sand also may be lower-cost viable options.
When ports must be dredged, the report said the Corps of Engineers' policies should be revised to favor options to re-use sediment for beneficial purposes, even if those options are not the cheapest.

For example, it said at the Port of Tacoma, Washington, contaminated dredge material was placed in a containment facility, capped with clean materials, and used as a base for waterfront real estate and a tidal mudflat.

The report also said the Corps of Engineers and the EPA should expand their support of research, development and demonstration of new technologies for assessing, dredging and treating contaminated sites.
